accuracy.evidence: Facts checked against National Geographic Kids and BBC Bitesize KS1 habitat pages: the Arctic and Antarctica are cold and icy, a rainforest is hot with rain on most days, a hot desert gets very little rain, polar bears live only in the Arctic, wild penguins live in the southern hemisphere, camels in hot deserts, parrots in rainforest canopy and shore crabs in rock pools. The lab always says 'hot desert' so it never claims every desert is hot, and the Arctic town is drawn with brightly painted houses as in Greenland, with no tall trees.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the polar confusions young children show (penguins living with polar bears, penguins only in zoos), 'hot means dry' for rainforests, 'deserts are rainy or full of trees', and the people stereotypes the brief flagged: 'nobody lives in the Arctic' and 'everyone lives in igloos'. The adult text names these mistakes and asks parents to be careful with stereotypes about how other families live.

lab_distinct.evidence: No other lab in the repo models environments: a hot/cold drag sort of four place scenes, a seven-day weather diary with rain jars comparing rainforest and desert, an animal-to-habitat drag onto four drawn landscapes, a same-or-different judgement between Sam's town and an Arctic town, and two mystery places solved from staged clues that start ambiguous. The shingle gate passed against all other flag labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: Every step is the compare skill from the Early Learning Goal done by the child: decide hot or cold, see that two hot places differ in rain (6 rainy days against 0), match animal features to places, sort four statements into same or different, and reason from clues. The mystery step refuses a correct guess after only the sand clue and says why, so the child learns one clue can fit two places.

predictions.evidence: Five locked predictions with plausible distractors: which place is cold all year (hot desert listed first), which hot place gets most rain ('They get the same' is the trap), where polar bears live, whether people live in the Arctic ('Only in igloos'), and where a sandy clue could be ('Only the hot desert'). Each reveal states the result the lab just showed and names the child's choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven questions with fourteen slip tags, each answered with the fact that fixes it, e.g. penguin: 'Polar bears live in the far north. Wild penguins live in the south, many near Antarctica, so they never meet.' and igloo: 'Most people in the Arctic live in houses, like Sam does.' In-lab errors (wrong side, wrong habitat, wrong same/different, guesses that break a clue) each get their own explanation.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences of familiar words (hot, cold, ice, sand, rain, trees) and score well under the family FK limit; the adult text was rewritten into shorter sentences and passes the 10.0 limit. Precise early-years terms are used: environment, contrasting environments, compare, similarities and differences, and the place names Arctic, Antarctica, hot desert, rainforest and seaside.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler scan and the explanation-overlap gate. Each kid paragraph covers a different place pair or the people comparison, and the adult paragraphs cover in turn the curriculum link, the words to model, the named mistakes and a description of the lab, with no repeated sentences.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots after Show me on every step at Android 360 px dark and iPhone 13 light: place scenes fit the 2x2 grid, the badges stay inside the canvas, and the weather icons were enlarged after the first pass. Place choices are full-width lbtn buttons that wrap on narrow screens. The same/different list was switched to the main text colour so it stays readable on the pale light-theme panel.

accessibility.evidence: The browser gate ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA on desktop and iPhone 13 in both themes with no violations and no console errors. All canvas labels sit on badges filled with the theme panel colour and stroked in the text colour, so contrast holds over bright scene art. Every drag has a button twin with an aria-label such as 'Take the camel to the Hot desert' or 'Put Arctic on the cold side', and the canvas aria-label tracks each spoken message.
